renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: ps_curve
  title: Contact probability against distance
  description: |-
    Each line is a chromosome, plus the genome-wide pooled curve: the probability that two loci a given distance apart are in contact, on log axes. It answers how fast contacts decay with genomic distance.
    How to read: contacts fall steadily with distance. Chromosomes whose curve departs from the pooled one carry a different folding or a technical bias, and a plateau or bump at long range can point to translocations or poor balancing. Open the slope view for the local decay rate.
    Note: this is the tool's expected contact table re-binned over log-spaced distances, with no cut-off drawn.
  kind: profile
  config:
    log_x: true
    log_y: true
    x_title: Genomic distance (bp)
    y_title: Contact probability
  roles:
    series: chrom
    x: distance
    y: contact_probability

- component: advanced_viz
  id: ps_slope
  title: Slope of the contact decay
  description: |-
    Each line is a chromosome, plus the genome-wide pooled curve: the local slope of the contact probability against distance, on log axes. It answers at which distance scales the decay changes.
    How to read: a steady slope means a single regime of folding. A change of slope marks a scale where the organisation changes, such as the footprint of loop extrusion, and a chromosome off the others needs a closer look.
    Note: the slope is a derivative of a noisy curve, so it is unreliable at the largest distances where few pairs of bins are left. No cut-off is drawn.
  kind: profile
  config:
    log_x: true
    x_title: Genomic distance (bp)
    y_title: Log-log slope of the contact probability
  roles:
    series: chrom
    x: distance
    y: log10_slope

- component: card
  title: Decay slope of the pooled curve
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median log-log slope of the genome-wide contact curve, and the box shows how the slope varies across distances. It answers how steeply contacts fall off overall.
    How to read: a more negative slope means contacts are lost faster with distance. Compare samples or resolutions, as the value shifts with both.
  column: log10_slope
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  filter_expr: col('chrom') == 'all'
  caption: median log-log slope of the pooled curve, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Short-range contact probability
  description: |-
    The hero number is the highest contact probability of the genome-wide curve, found at the shortest distance, and the strip shows its median and lowest value. It answers how strong the contacts are at short range and how far they fall.
    How to read: the maximum and the minimum differ by orders of magnitude on every Hi-C map. A change of the maximum between samples points to a different sequencing depth or resolution rather than to biology.
  column: contact_probability
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  - min
  secondary_layout: vertical
  filter_expr: col('chrom') == 'all'
  caption: highest contact probability of the pooled curve, with its median and lowest

- component: table
  title: Contact probability per distance
  description: |-
    Each row is a distance bin of a chromosome with its contact probability, log slope, observed contacts and number of possible bin pairs. It answers the exact values behind the curves.
    How to read: filter the chromosome column to one chromosome or to the pooled curve and sort by distance.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_track
  title: TAD domains along the genome
  description: |-
    Each rectangle is a domain, drawn from its start to its end on a chromosome-aware axis, at a height equal to its size in kilobases. It answers how the genome is partitioned into topological domains and how large they are.
    How to read: neighbouring rectangles of similar height are a regular partition. Very large domains often span poorly mappable regions or centromeres, and a run of very small ones suggests noise in the boundary calls.
    Note: domains are derived from the insulation boundary calls, so they change with the window size and the boundary threshold.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    mark: rect
    score_title: Domain size (kb)
  roles:
    chr: chrom
    pos: start
    score: size_kb
    end: end
    sample: sample

- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_size_track
  title: TAD domain size track
  description: |-
    Each segment is a domain on its chromosome, with its size in kilobases on the vertical axis. It answers the same question as the domain track with a Plotly renderer.
    How to read: compare the sizes along a chromosome and between samples. A consistent size range means a stable partition, and isolated very tall segments mark unusually large domains.
  kind: coverage_track
  config:
    color_by: sample
  roles:
    chromosome: chrom
    position: start
    value: size_kb
    end: end
    sample: sample

- component: card
  title: Domain size
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median size of a domain in kilobases, and the box shows how sizes spread. It answers how large the topological domains are.
    How to read: the median depends on the window size and on the resolution, so compare samples at the same settings. A long upper whisker means a few very large domains.
  column: size_kb
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median domain size in kilobases, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Domains per chromosome
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of domains, and the bars rank the chromosomes that hold most of them. It answers how the domains are spread over the genome.
    How to read: the leaders should be the longest chromosomes. A short one among them means smaller domains or noisier boundary calls there.
  column: size_kb
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: chrom
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: domains in view, with the chromosomes holding most ranked

- component: card
  title: Mappable share of a domain
  description: |-
    The hero number is the average share of a domain's bins that hold usable data, and the histogram shows how the domains spread. It answers how much of the domain calls rest on mappable sequence.
    How to read: values close to one are well supported. A pile at low values means many domains sit across unmappable regions, so their edges are less reliable.
  column: valid_fraction
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - min
  - median
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: average share of valid bins, with the lowest and the median

- component: table
  title: TAD domains
  description: |-
    Each row is a domain with its chromosome, start, end, size, number of bins, valid fraction and the boundary strength at its two edges. It answers the exact coordinates and support of every domain.
    How to read: sort by size or by edge strength to find the largest and the best supported domains.

- component: card
  title: First eigenvalue
  description: |-
    The hero number is the average first eigenvalue, the amount of the intra-chromosomal structure the first eigenvector explains, and the box shows how chromosomes spread. It answers how strongly each chromosome separates into two compartments.
    How to read: a chromosome with a much lower value than the others has a weak compartment signal, so its compartment track is less reliable.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/eigdecomp.py
  column: eigval1
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: average first eigenvalue, with its spread over chromosomes

- component: card
  title: Second eigenvalue
  description: |-
    The hero number is the range of the second eigenvalue and the box shows how chromosomes spread. It answers how much structure the next eigenvector explains beyond the compartments.
    How to read: a second eigenvalue close to the first means the compartment signal is not the dominant structure of that chromosome. The sign of an eigenvalue is not meaningful on its own, so the range is shown.
  column: eigval2
  aggregation: range
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: range of the second eigenvalue, with its spread over chromosomes

- component: table
  title: Eigenvalues per chromosome
  description: |-
    Each row is a chromosome at a resolution with its first three eigenvalues. It answers the exact values behind the cards.
    How to read: sort by the first eigenvalue to find the chromosomes with the weakest compartment signal.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: compartment_track
  title: A/B compartment track
  description: |-
    Each point is a bin of a chromosome with its first eigenvector value, coloured by compartment. It answers which parts of the genome are in the active A compartment and which in the inactive B compartment.
    How to read: positive values are A and negative values are B, and the zero-crossings are compartment boundaries. Long alternating stretches that match the expected pattern mean a clean decomposition, and an inverted chromosome arm is worth a check.
    Lines and annotations: the compartment labels are this catalog's convention, A for positive E1 and B for negative. The recipe phases each chromosome so that E1 correlates positively with bin coverage, the better-covered compartment being A, the same way at every resolution. The cooltools documentation instead orients E1 to correlate positively with GC content, the usual convention for Hi-C.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/eigdecomp.py and https://cooltools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/compartments_and_saddles.html
  kind: coverage_track
  config:
    color_by: category
  roles:
    chromosome: chrom
    position: start
    value: E1
    category: compartment

- component: advanced_viz
  id: compartment_locus_track
  title: A/B compartments on the genome axis
  description: |-
    Each mark is a bin with its E1 value, coloured by compartment on a chromosome-aware axis. It answers the same question as the track with a view that lines up with the insulation and domain tracks.
    How to read: zoom into a boundary and compare it with the TAD boundaries of the other tracks. Compartment boundaries often coincide with domain boundaries.
    Lines and annotations: the compartment labels are this catalog's convention, A for positive E1 and B for negative.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/eigdecomp.py
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    score_title: First eigenvector (E1)
  roles:
    chr: chrom
    pos: start
    score: E1
    end: end
    sample: sample
    category: compartment

- component: card
  title: Compartment signal
  description: |-
    The hero number is the range of the first eigenvector over all bins, and the box shows how its values spread. It answers how strong the compartment signal is.
    How to read: a box centred on zero with long whiskers on both sides is a balanced A and B pattern. A box shifted to one side means an unbalanced decomposition or a poorly phased chromosome.
  column: E1
  aggregation: range
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: range of E1, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Share of A and B bins
  description: |-
    Each unit is a bin with an E1 value and the ring splits them into the A and B compartments. It answers what share of the mappable genome is active.
    How to read: a roughly balanced ring is typical. A large imbalance suggests a sign problem in one chromosome, so check the track.
  column: E1
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: donut
  breakdown_col: compartment
  caption: bins with an E1 value, split by compartment

- component: table
  title: Eigenvector values per bin
  description: |-
    Each row is a bin with its coordinates, balancing weight, first three eigenvector values and compartment. It answers the exact value behind every track.
    How to read: filter by chromosome and sort by start to read a region.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: insulation_track
  title: Insulation score track
  description: |-
    Each point is a bin of a chromosome with its log2 insulation score, one line per sample. It answers where the local contact structure is broken into domains.
    How to read: dips of the score mark TAD boundaries, where contacts across the bin are depleted. Sharp, deep dips are strong boundaries and shallow ones are weak.
    Lines and annotations: boundaries are called by cooltools on the boundary strength, with the Li threshold by default. They are listed in the table and in the boundary card.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  kind: coverage_track
  config:
    color_by: sample
  roles:
    chromosome: chrom
    position: start
    value: log2_insulation_score
    sample: sample

- component: advanced_viz
  id: insulation_locus_track
  title: Insulation on the genome axis
  description: |-
    Each mark is a bin with its log2 insulation score on a chromosome-aware axis. It answers the same question as the track with a view that stacks under the contact map.
    How to read: zoom into a dip and compare it with the compartment and domain tracks. A boundary shared between tracks is a robust one.
    Lines and annotations: no score line is drawn, as boundaries are called on the boundary strength and not on this score.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    score_title: Log2 insulation score
  roles:
    chr: chrom
    pos: start
    score: log2_insulation_score
    end: end
    sample: sample

- component: card
  title: Insulation score
  description: |-
    The hero number is the range of the log2 insulation score over all bins, and the box shows how it spreads. It answers how deep the dips are compared with the rest of the genome.
    How to read: a wide range with a box close to zero is a track with clear boundaries. A narrow range means weak insulation or a window that is too wide for the resolution.
  column: log2_insulation_score
  aggregation: range
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: range of the log2 insulation score, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Boundary strength
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median strength of the boundaries cooltools called, and the strip shows the weakest and the strongest. It answers how well defined the boundaries are.
    How to read: a few very strong boundaries over many weak ones is the usual shape. Compare the strongest ones between samples to see changes of domain organisation.
    Lines and annotations: cooltools keeps the boundaries above a threshold on their strength, Li by default or Otsu or a fixed value on request.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  column: boundary_strength
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: vertical
  caption: median strength of the called boundaries, with the weakest and strongest

- component: card
  title: Boundary bins
  description: |-
    Each unit is a bin with an insulation score and the ring splits them into called boundaries and the rest. It answers what share of the genome sits on a boundary.
    How to read: boundaries should be a small share of the bins. A large share means a permissive threshold or a window too small for the resolution.
    Lines and annotations: a bin is a boundary when its strength passes the threshold cooltools applies, Li by default.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  column: log2_insulation_score
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: donut
  breakdown_col: is_boundary
  caption: bins with a score, split by boundary call

- component: table
  title: Insulation per bin
  description: |-
    Each row is a bin at one window size with its insulation score, boundary strength and boundary call. It answers the exact values behind the tracks.
    How to read: filter to called boundaries and sort by strength to list the best defined ones.

    score_title: Log2 insulation score
  roles:
    chr: chrom
    pos: start
    score: log2_insulation_score
    end: end
    sample: sample

- component: card
  title: Insulation score
  description: |-
    The hero number is the range of the log2 insulation score over all bins, and the box shows how it spreads. It answers how deep the dips are compared with the rest of the genome.
    How to read: a wide range with a box close to zero is a track with clear boundaries. A narrow range means weak insulation or a window that is too wide for the resolution.
  column: log2_insulation_score
  aggregation: range
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: range of the log2 insulation score, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Boundary strength
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median strength of the boundaries cooltools called, and the strip shows the weakest and the strongest. It answers how well defined the boundaries are.
    How to read: a few very strong boundaries over many weak ones is the usual shape. Compare the strongest ones between samples to see changes of domain organisation.
    Lines and annotations: cooltools keeps the boundaries above a threshold on their strength, Li by default or Otsu or a fixed value on request.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  column: boundary_strength
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: vertical
  caption: median strength of the called boundaries, with the weakest and strongest

- component: card
  title: Boundary bins
  description: |-
    Each unit is a bin with an insulation score and the ring splits them into called boundaries and the rest. It answers what share of the genome sits on a boundary.
    How to read: boundaries should be a small share of the bins. A large share means a permissive threshold or a window too small for the resolution.
    Lines and annotations: a bin is a boundary when its strength passes the threshold cooltools applies, Li by default.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  column: log2_insulation_score
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: donut
  breakdown_col: is_boundary
  caption: bins with a score, split by boundary call

- component: table
  title: Insulation per bin
  description: |-
    Each row is a bin at one window size with its insulation score, boundary strength and boundary call. It answers the exact values behind the tracks.
    How to read: filter to called boundaries and sort by strength to list the best defined ones.
